title: The Future of South American Militaries and Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief Operations
text:
The Future of South American Militaries and Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief Operations

Photo: NELSON ALMEIDA/AFP via Getty Images

Commentary
by

Wilder Alejandro Sánchez

Published November 19, 2026

The end of 2026 and early 2027 will be a challenging period for South American militaries. Their primary mission will remain unchanged: to be ready to defend their respective nations from external threats. At the same time, armed forces will also need sufficient capabilities to combat domestic irregular threats such as drug trafficking networks, narco-insurgents and their deadly drones, illegal mining, and environmental crimes including illegal fishing and wildlife trafficking. While preparing for interstate conflict and fighting domestic criminals and insurgents are priorities for the armed services, another regional, ever-present threat exists that cannot be defeated with conventional weapons: natural disasters.The region is already prone to wildfires, droughts, torrential rains, and other extreme weather patterns and disasters, but climate change will worsen them. Weather forecasts predict a super El Niño in the coming months, which could be particularly devastating for South American countries. The region already has a long history of deadly and destructive natural disasters, including devastating earthquakes in Colombia, Panama, and Venezuela within the past six months, making the threat of a super El Niño especially urgent when considering broader regional security implications.The tip of the proverbial spear to protect local populations will be South American armed forces, which will be deployed in significant numbers in the coming months to support populations and address natural disasters as part of humanitarian assistance and disaster relief (HA/DR) operations. Recent floods in Ecuador’s Galápagos Islands, northern Peru, and Paraguay, as well as wildfires in Brazil, are early signs of what could be a very problematic summer for countries south of the equator.Recent OperationsIn recent weeks, massive storms have caused severe flooding across South America, while wildfires simultaneously affect other parts of the continent. The situation is expected to worsen as the southern hemisphere’s summer months arrive. Recent military HA/DR operations help explain the urgency of preparing for environmental disasters, the need to improve the capacities of local civilian agencies, and how military forces can respond.Heavy rains in northern Peru have flooded many areas. To help the affected populations, many units and assets have been deployed—for example, troops assigned to Artillery Group Crl. José Joaquín Inclán of the Peruvian Army brought rice, blankets, and other aid to the municipality of San Juan de Bigote, Piura region, helping affected families. Meanwhile, a field hospital was set up by the Army’s 9th Armor Brigade in Tumbes region to help medical services cope with any outbreaks of dengue that may affect the local population; troops from the same unit are also busy unclogging and cleaning water canals. Peruvian marines, a component of the Navy, armed with shovels, buckets, and thick boots, have also been deployed to Tumbes to help clean the streets.Meanwhile, in Paraguay, the Paraná River overflowed, affecting communities in the Cerrito municipality, Ñeembucú department. As part of an immediate disaster response, a 6x6 truck assigned to the Paraguayan Army’s Cavalry Regiment No. 4 transported food to the local population. The truck helped distribute kits to zones that “were flooded, isolated, or difficult to enter,” demonstrating the military’s essential role in disaster operations beyond civilian capacity. Moreover, three small riverine craft operated by military personnel were also deployed.In Ecuador, heavy rains flooded the Galápagos Islands, especially the inhabited Santa Cruz Island, requiring a joint-force response. The Coast Guard patrol vessel Isla San Cristóbal transported over 10 tons of food, blankets, medicine, mattresses, hoses, and other equipment from the mainland to the island. The transport vessel Imbabura was also deployed to Santa Cruz with medicine, food, stoves, water, and a power generator. Meanwhile, Air Force personnel are in the Galápagos helping people move their personal belongings from their homes and maintaining security in the streets. The service is also using a C-130 Hercules transport aircraft to move equipment and other aid.While some parts of South America have too much water, others are being destroyed by wildfires. In Brazil, the government, including the armed forces, is battling wildfires in Amazonas state. Since October 12, the government, including defense agencies, has dropped a reported one million liters of water to combat the wildfires; around 250 military personnel from the Army, Air Force, and Navy are helping with the mission. The equipment and platforms deployed include two KC-390 Millennium multirole aircraft (Air Force), a UH-15 Super Cougar helicopter (Navy), and one HM-1A Pantera helicopter (Army) that transport both personnel and equipment. The KC-390s were “configured” for firefighting operations by carrying the Modular Airborne Firefighting System and Compressed Air Foam System.Similarly, Chile, a country known for massive and destructive wildfires, is already preparing to combat them this upcoming summer. At the end of October, President José Antonio Kast led a conference at Tobalaba Airport to unveil and launch the Plan de Protección contra Incendios Forestales 2026–2027, a government plan to fight forest fires this summer. The armed forces were represented by Minister of Defense Fernando Barros, who emphasized the military’s work to anticipate, plan, and prepare for what could be “a difficult wildfire season.” In years past, in addition to personnel and platforms such as helicopters and aircraft, the armed forces have also used drones for reconnaissance missions during forest fires.Looking ForwardWhen a disaster occurs, police and other law enforcement forces, medical services, firefighters, and other services also play critical roles. In several South American countries, special agencies are specifically tasked with managing disasters, such as Peru’s Instituto Nacional de Defensa Civil, Colombia’s Defensa Civil Colombiana, and Brazil’s Secretaria Nacional de Proteção e Defesa Civil. However, because of their organization and access to a variety of assets and platforms, armed forces will remain the cornerstone of future HA/DR missions.Therefore, personnel training and the acquisition of necessary equipment must be addressed to improve local armed forces’ disaster relief response. Some armed forces have created multipurpose units specifically trained for HA/DR missions. The Peruvian armed forces, for example, have established rapid reaction companies specifically trained, equipped, and organized for humanitarian operations. Similarly, the Colombian Army has a specialized brigade for these missions. Looking forward, regional forces may need to increase the size of HA/DR units and formations.Next is the question of equipment, besides existing search-and-rescue equipment, medical equipment, ambulances, and portable field hospitals. Aircraft such as the C-130 Hercules or the Brazilian-built C-390 Millennium can help armed forces transport personnel, equipment, and food and evacuate casualties. Similarly, ground vehicles such as trucks can also support ground operations. For naval forces, multipurpose transport vessels can serve as hospitals and transport large amounts of equipment, food, water, and medicines to disaster-hit coastal areas. These specialized types of transport equipment are a critical component to maximize armed forces’ HA/DR response capabilities. Additionally, HA/DR response equipment is multipurpose and strengthens regular military operations. Moving forward, armed services and defense ministries can leverage this multipurpose use to justify additional budget requests.Regional armed forces are already prioritizing the acquisition of equipment that can support HA/DR missions as well as military operations. In recent years, Peru’s SIMA shipyard has built two landing docks, Pisco and Paita, and recently launched two support vessels, Chimbote and Talara; Chile’s ASMAR shipyard is building two multipurpose vessels, Magallanes and Rapa Nui. Regarding regional air forces, Brazil’s domestically manufactured C-390 already supports aerial HA/DR missions, Argentina is acquiring helicopters that can transport Bambi buckets to combat wildfires, and Peru has acquired Textron Beechcraft King Air 360C aircraft to transport equipment and conduct medical evacuations.A final issue regarding equipment is the potential acquisition of new technologies to support future HA/DR missions. Small ground robots can support search-and-rescue missions by entering collapsed structures to look for survivors without putting rescuers in danger. Similarly, aerial drones can provide a cheap but effective bird’s-eye view of an area affected by flooding or mudslides and can inspect the size of a wildfire.HA/DR missions also have one curious, but positive, effect: They are confidence-building mechanisms for regional governments and militaries. When a disaster occurs, state armed forces often deploy aircraft with aid, search-and-rescue personnel, doctors, or helicopters with Bambi buckets to support neighboring states. This cooperation strengthens military relations, builds new friendships, and arguably reduces the likelihood of tensions that could escalate into interstate conflict.The Inter-American Defense Board (IADB) recently hosted a conference on HA/DR missions. Captain Marcelo Eduardo Apolo Kubes from Ecuador’s Navy explained in his remarks at the conference that, to improve partnerships and cooperation in HA/DR, the 2020 conference of Western Hemisphere ministers of defense “recommended the IADB to establish a mechanism” for HA/DR cooperation, now called the Directorate of the Mechanism for Cooperation during Disasters (MECODE). “Solidarity is never lacking. However, the aid does not always align with the actual needs of the moment,” Captain Apolo Kubes explained. Hence, mechanisms like MECODE or the SICODE program, also known as the Cooperation System During Disasters, are meant to promote dialogue, training, and actual coordination and communication when a disaster occurs.Concerns and Next Steps for South American MilitariesThe ongoing, and potentially increasing, role of South American armed forces in HA/DR missions also raises questions and concerns about the future. First, troops may be overextended because they must carry out many missions simultaneously. South American militaries are not particularly numerous; hence, creating HA/DR–focused formations such as battalions and companies can be problematic. While all armed service personnel must be ready for combat operations, focusing the training of dozens or hundreds of troops on HA/DR missions means they will not be trained or readily available to carry out other combat missions. With the creation of dedicated HA/DR units, countries must question the quantity of resources and required recruitment for them. Furthermore, considerations must also include whether such formations would strengthen the overall capabilities of existing armed forces.Another concern is the equipment itself. As the previous section noted, South American naval forces are acquiring multipurpose vessels that can serve both combat and HA/DR operations. The modernization is mandatory; however, with limited budgets, the question remains whether naval commands prioritize acquiring multipurpose vessels over, for example, new combat surface ships or submarines to maintain minimal deterrence capabilities in case of interstate tensions.Ultimately, the larger question is overreliance on armed forces for noncombat operations. Law enforcement agencies and other nonmilitary security services are primarily tasked with domestic security operations such as combating narco-insurgents and drug traffickers, cracking down on illegal mining, and daily street patrols to improve citizen security, while military personnel are supposed to train primarily to protect the nation from foreign threats. In reality, however, South American militaries are deployed to fight alongside law enforcement agencies, and often instead of those agencies, within their nation’s territory.The same situation can be applied to HA/DR missions. Ideally, each country should have a strong civilian disaster management office with sufficient personnel and its own equipment, such as helicopters capable of transporting Bambi buckets, to avoid overrelying on military platforms and troops. Without a doubt, when a natural disaster occurs, local armed forces would certainly participate to support their fellow citizens. Nevertheless, the question is whether certain HA/DR missions would be more effective if civilian agencies were better funded and had more personnel and equipment, so they would not have to rely too much on the armed services.While the courage of military personnel to combat wildfires or rescue citizens affected by floods cannot be questioned, the growing role of South American militaries in HA/DR missions deserves a wider discussion about governments overrelying on armed forces for noncombat operations. The future makeup of the services themselves should also be considered. Their role in HA/DR operations mean that regional armed forces are tasked with additional and long-enduring missions that will put stress on services with a limited number of troops, budget, and equipment.South American armies, air forces, and navies will be heavily involved in response to future natural disasters across the region, which are expected to be particularly severe due to the upcoming super El Niño. Still, the question is whether armed forces should remain the tip of the HA/DR spear, or whether civilian agencies should be better equipped, staffed, and budgeted to take over the primary role in these operations.Wilder Alejandro Sánchez is a senior associate (non-resident) with the Americas Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, D.C.
